section.title: Joseph and Potiphar's House
section.sectionRationale: Sold into Egypt, Joseph rises in Potiphar's house because the LORD is with him. When his master's wife tempts him, he refuses out of loyalty and reverence for God, and is falsely accused and imprisoned, yet the LORD is with him still. The chapter is framed by the refrain of God's abiding presence.
section.thesis: The LORD's presence, not outward circumstance, is the true blessing; He prospers His faithful servant in a slave's house and a prison cell alike, sustaining integrity under temptation and injustice on the road to a saving purpose.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the LORD with Joseph in Potiphar's house; the temptation resisted; the false accusation and imprisonment; and the LORD with Joseph in prison.

verses.text: Meanwhile, Joseph had been taken down to Egypt, where an Egyptian named Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there.
And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a {{tsalach|successful}} man, serving in the household of his Egyptian master.
When his master saw that the LORD was with him and made him prosper in all he did,
Joseph found {{chen|favor}} in his sight and became his personal attendant. Potiphar put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned.

From the time that he put Joseph in charge of his household and all he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him. The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field.
So Potiphar left all that he owned in Joseph’s care; he did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was well-built and handsome,

units.label: Temptation resisted
units.note: how could I sin against God

verses.text: and after some time his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Sleep with me.”
But he refused. “Look,” he said to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master does not concern himself with anything in his house, and he has entrusted everything he owns to my care.
No one in this house is greater than I am. He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and {{chata|sin against God}}?”
Although Potiphar’s wife spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be near her.
One day, however, Joseph went into the house to attend to his work, and not a single household servant was inside.
She grabbed Joseph by his {{beged|cloak}} and said, “Sleep with me!” But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.

units.label: False accusation and prison
units.note: the cloak used as a lie

verses.text: When she saw that he had left his cloak in her hand and had run out of the house,
she called her household servants. “Look,” she said, “this Hebrew has been brought to us to make sport of us. He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could.
When he heard me scream for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.”
So Potiphar’s wife kept Joseph’s cloak beside her until his master came home.
Then she told him the same story: “The Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make sport of me,
but when I screamed for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.”
When his master heard the story his wife told him, saying, “This is what your slave did to me,” he burned with anger.
So Joseph’s master took him and had him thrown into the prison where the king’s prisoners were confined. While Joseph was there in the prison,

units.label: The LORD with Joseph in prison

verses.text: the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
And the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph’s care, so that he was responsible for all that was done in the prison.
The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.

tsalach.gloss: To succeed, prosper, or accomplish. In this chapter it describes Joseph in slavery and in prison, not in comfort. His prospering is not freedom from hardship but the fruitfulness God grants a faithful servant even in bondage, because the LORD is with him.

chen.gloss: Favor or grace, the goodwill one finds in another's eyes. Joseph gains favor with Potiphar and later with the prison warden, but the source is named plainly: the LORD grants it. The word points beyond human liking to the gracious hand of God who lifts the lowly.

chata.gloss: To sin, to miss the mark. Joseph names adultery not merely as a betrayal of Potiphar but as a great evil and sin against God Himself. His conscience is governed by the LORD's presence, showing that true purity flows from reverence for God, not just fear of getting caught.

beged.gloss: A garment or cloak. For the second time a garment of Joseph's is stripped away and used to lie about him, first the robe dipped in blood, now the cloak left in the woman's hand. The repeated motif marks Joseph as the falsely accused sufferer whose innocence God will vindicate.

basic.context: Joseph is now a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian official. Because the LORD is with him, he prospers and is put in charge of the whole household. When Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him, he refuses. She falsely accuses him, and he is thrown into prison, where again the LORD is with him and gives him favor.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is what it means that the LORD was with Joseph, since his life goes from slavery to false imprisonment. The chapter answers that God's presence is the real blessing, sustaining Joseph's integrity and fruitfulness even when his circumstances are unjust and hard.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for successful describes Joseph in slavery and prison, not ease. He finds favor, but the text says God grants it. Joseph calls adultery a sin against God, not just against his master. And once more a garment of his, his cloak, is seized and used to lie about him, marking him as the falsely accused.
basic.typology: Joseph is a clear type of Christ: the righteous servant who suffers unjustly, resists evil, is falsely accused, and is numbered with prisoners, yet is with God and finally vindicated. His purity and his descent into the prison prefigure the sinless Sufferer who goes down before He is raised.
basic.christ: Like Joseph, Jesus was the righteous one who did no wrong, was falsely accused, and was handed over to suffering, yet God was with Him throughout. Joseph's refusal to sin points to Christ's perfect obedience, and his unjust imprisonment points to the greater descent of the innocent Savior.
basic.god: The refrain the LORD was with Joseph frames the whole chapter. God is present in the slave quarters and in the dungeon, granting favor, blessing, and success. His presence does not remove hardship but transforms it, proving that nearness to God, not comfort, is the deepest good.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 105 says God tested Joseph until his word came true. Romans 8 promises that God works all things for good and that nothing can separate us from His love. Hebrews 13 assures believers that God will never leave nor forsake them.
basic.oneStory: Joseph's faithful suffering is one more step on the road by which God will raise him to save many. His integrity under temptation and his innocence under accusation display the character of the coming Redeemer, and the abiding presence of the God who is with His people in every pit.

context.literary:
Genesis 39 is one of the most carefully framed chapters in the book. The phrase 'the LORD was with Joseph' opens the story in verse 2 and closes it in verses 21 and 23, and it appears again in verse 3 on the lips of the narrator describing what Potiphar saw. The chapter falls into three movements that the frame holds together: Joseph's rise in Potiphar's house, verses 1 to 6; the temptation and the false charge, verses 7 to 20; and Joseph's rise in the prison, verses 21 to 23. The first and last movements match closely. In each, Joseph is placed over everything, the man in charge 'did not concern himself with anything,' verses 6 and 23, and the reason is the LORD. Between those two panels stands the crisis.

The middle section builds with repetition. Potiphar's wife speaks 'day after day,' verse 10. Her demand is the same two words each time, 'Sleep with me,' verses 7 and 12. Then the story slows to linger over one object, Joseph's cloak. It is grabbed, left, held, displayed to the servants, kept beside her, and shown to her husband, verses 12 to 18. As in chapter 37, a garment taken from Joseph becomes false evidence about him, and the narrator lets the reader see the lie form.

The chapter resumes the story broken off at Genesis 37:36, and verse 1 deliberately repeats that verse's wording. Chapter 38 stands in between, and the placement invites comparison. Judah, free and at home, goes to a woman on the road; Joseph, a slave in a foreign house, refuses his master's wife. Judah is exposed by his own seal and staff; Joseph is falsely accused by means of his own cloak. The two chapters together show the two brothers who will matter most in the rest of Genesis, one beginning a long repentance, the other holding fast.

Within the larger Joseph story, chapter 39 is the lowest point before the turn. Joseph descends from favoured son to slave to prisoner, and the next chapters will bring him from the prison to Pharaoh's side, Genesis 41:41-43.
context.historical:
Potiphar is called 'an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard,' verse 1. The narrator also calls him 'an Egyptian' three times, verses 1, 2 and 5, which underlines that Joseph is now a foreign slave in a foreign household. His name is Egyptian and is usually explained as meaning 'the one whom Ra has given,' close to the name Potiphera, the priest of On whose daughter Joseph later marries, Genesis 41:45.

A wealthy Egyptian household included land, fields, livestock and many servants, and a capable slave could rise to become steward over the whole estate. Joseph's promotion to the one in charge 'of his household and all he owned,' verse 4, fits this well. The note that Potiphar concerned himself with nothing 'except the food he ate,' verse 6, may simply mean he trusted Joseph with everything else. It may also reflect Egyptian food customs, since Genesis 43:32 says the Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews, so that Joseph would have been kept out of the kitchen.

The accusation plays on ethnic contempt. She calls Joseph 'this Hebrew' and 'the Hebrew slave,' verses 14 and 17, the same term used of 'Abram the Hebrew,' Genesis 14:13, but here spoken as a sneer. She also shifts blame onto her husband: 'this Hebrew has been brought to us,' and to him, 'The Hebrew slave you brought us.' She rallies the servants against an outsider and puts Potiphar on the defensive at the same time.

Adultery was treated as a grave wrong throughout the ancient Near East. An Egyptian story known today as the Tale of Two Brothers has a married woman try to seduce her husband's younger brother and then falsely accuse him, which shows that the situation was one Egyptian readers would recognise. The punishment Potiphar chose was not death but prison, 'where the king's prisoners were confined,' verse 20, a royal holding place connected with Potiphar's own office, Genesis 40:3. That prison is where Joseph will meet Pharaoh's officials and the path to the throne will open.
context.canonical:
The chapter is echoed in the rest of Scripture mainly through its refrain and its outcome. The promise 'I am with you' ran through the patriarchs, to Isaac, Genesis 26:3, and to Jacob, Genesis 28:15, and now the narrator says it of Joseph without any appearance or vision. The same pattern marks later servants of God: 'he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him,' said of David, 1 Samuel 18:14, and God's word to Moses, 'I will surely be with you,' Exodus 3:12. Daniel, another young Hebrew in a foreign court, finds that 'God had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official,' Daniel 1:9, much as Joseph found favor with the prison warden.

Psalm 105:17-19 describes Joseph's imprisonment from God's side: 'They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons, until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.' Genesis 39 says nothing of chains; the psalm shows how hard the prison was and that it was a time of testing.

Proverbs gives extended warnings against the adulterous woman, whose lips 'drip honey' but whose end is 'bitter as wormwood,' Proverbs 5:3-4, and whose persuasion leads the simple man 'like an ox going to the slaughter,' Proverbs 7:21-22. Joseph is the living counter example, the young man who refuses.

In the New Testament Stephen summarises the whole period: 'God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom,' Acts 7:9-10. Paul's command 'Flee from sexual immorality,' 1 Corinthians 6:18, and his charge to Timothy to 'flee from youthful passions,' 2 Timothy 2:22, have often been read with Joseph in mind. Peter's teaching on enduring 'the pain of unjust suffering,' 1 Peter 2:19, fits Joseph's case exactly, and Peter grounds it in Christ, who 'committed no sin,' 1 Peter 2:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants Israel to understand what it means for God to be with His people. Israel would spend long years as slaves in Egypt and later as exiles in Babylon, often in circumstances that seemed to deny God's favour. This chapter shows that the LORD can be fully with His servant when that servant is a slave and when he is in prison, and that His presence shows itself in faithfulness, fruitfulness and favour rather than in escape.

He also wants his hearers to see what faithfulness looks like in the place of temptation. Joseph's refusal is not merely prudent. He gives reasons: loyalty to the master who trusted him, respect for the marriage, and above all accountability to God, 'how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?' verse 9. The first hearers are meant to learn that sin is first of all against God, and that fidelity to Him is worth more than safety or advancement.

And he wants them to see that doing right may bring suffering. Joseph does what is right and ends up in prison. The narrator does not soften that, and he does not explain it in this chapter. He simply frames it with God's presence and lets the rest of the story show where it leads. Israel was meant to learn patience: God's presence does not guarantee quick vindication, but it does guarantee that He has not abandoned His servant.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes Joseph's conduct rather than commanding it, but his conduct matches what God later commands. The seventh commandment, 'You shall not commit adultery,' Exodus 20:14, and the New Testament's 'Flee from sexual immorality,' 1 Corinthians 6:18, make Joseph's refusal a model to follow and not only a story to admire. His physical flight, leaving the cloak behind, shows that sometimes the only faithful response to temptation is to leave.

Other elements are simply recorded. Potiphar's wife's lies, Potiphar's anger and the injustice of the sentence are not approved. Joseph's silence under accusation is noted by its absence; the text gives him no speech of defence, and it does not ask readers to decide whether he should have spoken.

The prosperity Joseph enjoys is also descriptive. It shows what God did for Joseph, not a promise that every faithful believer will rise to be steward or overseer. What carries over is the pattern: God's people can serve well in hard places, bless the households and institutions they are placed in, and entrust the outcome to God, 1 Peter 2:23.

debates.question: Does the LORD was with Joseph mean God's people should expect outward success and ease?

views.label: Presence, not prosperity as comfort
views.case: Joseph prospers precisely while enslaved and imprisoned; the blessing is God's nearness and fruitfulness in hardship, not release from it. The refrain frames a chapter that ends in a prison, and Psalm 105:18 adds shackles and irons, ruling out a health-and-wealth reading.

views.label: God grants genuine favor and advancement
views.case: The text does show real, tangible favor: Joseph is elevated in the house and in the prison, and God visibly blesses what he touches, even blessing Potiphar's house on his account, verse 5, so God's presence often bears outward fruit, though never guaranteeing ease.

debates.bearing: Both agree the deepest good is God with us. Believers may trust God's real blessing and providence without expecting immunity from injustice, following Joseph's faithfulness whatever the outcome.

debates.question: Did Potiphar believe his wife's accusation?

views.label: He believed her and punished Joseph
views.case: The text says that when he heard his wife's story 'he burned with anger,' verse 19, and he immediately had Joseph imprisoned. A slave accused by the master's wife had no standing to defend himself, and Potiphar acted as any master would.

views.label: He had doubts and chose a lighter sentence
views.case: The text does not say whom Potiphar was angry with, and the punishment is surprisingly mild. A slave accused of assaulting his master's wife might expect death, yet Joseph is sent to the royal prison connected with Potiphar's own office, Genesis 40:3, where he is soon given responsibility. Some read this as a sign that Potiphar knew his wife and was not fully convinced, but had to act to save face.

debates.bearing: The narrator leaves Potiphar's mind unexplained and keeps the focus on the LORD, who is with Joseph in the prison as He was in the house. Whatever Potiphar thought, the sentence placed Joseph exactly where God would use him, next to Pharaoh's officials.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter uses the covenant name, the LORD, in its narration far more than the rest of the Joseph story does. 'The LORD was with Joseph,' verses 2, 21 and 23; 'the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household,' verse 5; 'the LORD's blessing was on everything he owned,' verse 5. Yet when Joseph speaks to Potiphar's wife he says 'sin against God,' Elohim, verse 9. The distinction is natural. The narrator speaks as one who knows Israel's covenant God, while Joseph speaks to an Egyptian in terms she could understand. The story is told from inside the covenant even though it takes place far outside the land.

'He became a successful man,' verse 2, uses the verb tsalach, to prosper or succeed, which returns in verses 3 and 23, 'gave him success in whatever he did.' The same verb describes the LORD making the servant's journey 'a success' in Genesis 24:21 and 24:40, and it later marks the one who meditates on God's law: 'then you will prosper and succeed,' Joshua 1:8, and 'who prospers in all he does,' Psalm 1:3. In every case the success is something God gives, not something the person achieves. Here it is given in a slave's quarters.

Joseph is 'well-built and handsome,' verse 6. The Hebrew phrase, beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance, is the same phrase used of his mother Rachel, 'shapely and beautiful,' Genesis 29:17. The son resembles the mother Jacob loved. The note also prepares for the danger: the next verse says that his master's wife 'cast her eyes upon Joseph,' literally lifted up her eyes, the look of desire.

Potiphar's wife says Joseph was brought 'to make sport of us,' verse 14, and 'to make sport of me,' verse 17. The verb is tsachaq, the root of Isaac's name, meaning to laugh, and in some forms to mock or to play. It is used when Ishmael was 'mocking' Isaac, Genesis 21:9, and when Isaac was 'caressing' Rebekah, Genesis 26:8. Her choice of word carries both sexual and insulting overtones, and it lets her accuse Joseph of the very thing she had attempted.

In verse 21 the LORD 'extended kindness to him.' The word is chesed, God's covenant loyalty and steadfast love. It is the word Abraham's servant praised God for, 'who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness,' Genesis 24:27, and the word Jacob used when he said, 'I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown,' Genesis 32:10. In the prison, where no human loyalty remains, God's chesed does. The verse adds that He gave Joseph 'favor,' chen, in the warden's eyes, the same word as in verse 4, 'Joseph found favor in his sight.' Daniel 1:9 uses chesed in a similar way for the favour God gave Daniel before a foreign official.

Finally, Potiphar is called 'an officer of Pharaoh,' verse 1. The word, saris, later often means a eunuch, and some have wondered whether that explains his wife's behaviour. But Potiphar is married, and the word is also used more broadly of a court official, which is how the BSB renders it. It is wise not to build on the narrower sense here.

typology.type: Joseph, the righteous servant falsely accused
typology.fulfillment: Joseph refuses sin, is accused by a lie built on his own cloak, and is condemned without a hearing. Jesus 'committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, yet the Sanhedrin sought 'false testimony against Jesus in order to put Him to death,' Matthew 26:59. Even the judge admitted, 'I find no basis for a charge against this man,' Luke 23:4. The escalation is that Joseph's silence may have been simply that of a slave with no voice, while Christ was silent by choice, entrusting Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. Joseph was innocent of one charge; Christ was sinless in every respect.

typology.type: Joseph numbered with the king's prisoners
typology.fulfillment: Joseph is thrown into the prison 'where the king's prisoners were confined,' verse 20, and is treated as a criminal among criminals, though he has done nothing wrong, Genesis 40:15. Isaiah 53:12 speaks of the Servant who 'was numbered with the transgressors,' and Jesus said, 'this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me,' Luke 22:37. He was crucified between two criminals. The escalation is that Christ was counted with sinners not only in location but in substance, since God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Joseph's prison led to Pharaoh's court; Christ's death led to the throne of God.

Joseph faced a persistent temptation, 'day after day,' verse 10, in a setting where no one would have known, and he refused out of loyalty to God. Christ 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and 'because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18. The escalation is that Joseph's integrity was one faithful act among others in a flawed life, while Christ's obedience was complete and unbroken. Joseph's refusal is an example; Christ's obedience is also the righteousness credited to those who trust Him.

typology.type: The master's house blessed on account of the servant
typology.fulfillment: 'The LORD blessed the Egyptian's household on account of him,' verse 5, a first taste of the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring, Genesis 12:3. Laban had already said the same of Jacob, Genesis 30:27. In Christ the blessing reaches its full measure: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, is fulfilled as Gentiles receive the blessing of Abraham in Christ Jesus, Galatians 3:14. The type falls short in that Potiphar's household received material blessing only, while in Christ the nations receive the promised Spirit.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the pattern of the righteous sufferer. Joseph is innocent; he refuses the evil that is urged on him day after day; he is accused by a lie built from his own garment; he is condemned without being allowed to speak; and he is placed among the king's prisoners. Every part of that sequence is found again in the passion of Jesus. He 'committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, quoting Isaiah 53:9. False witnesses came forward against Him, Matthew 26:59-60. His own garments were taken and divided, Matthew 27:35. He was 'numbered with the transgressors,' Luke 22:37. And like Joseph He did not answer the lie with a lie: 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23.

It leads to Christ by the theme of God's presence. The refrain 'the LORD was with Joseph' finds its fullest meaning in the one called 'Immanuel,' which means 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. Peter summarised Jesus' ministry by saying He went around doing good 'because God was with Him,' Acts 10:38. On the night of His arrest Jesus said, 'you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me,' John 16:32. Joseph experienced the presence of God in a prison; Jesus is the presence of God come into the world, and He promises His people, 'surely I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20.

It leads to Christ, too, by the theme of blessing through the servant. The LORD blessed Potiphar's house 'on account of' Joseph, verse 5, and the warden's prison flourished under him. The promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed through his seed, Genesis 12:3, is tasted here in one Egyptian household. It is fulfilled in Christ, 'so that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:14.

And it leads to Christ by the shape of the whole story. Joseph's descent from slave to prisoner is the lowest point before his exaltation to ride in Pharaoh's second chariot, with men calling out before him, 'Bow the knee!' Genesis 41:43. Christ's descent went further, into death itself, and His exaltation is higher: 'God exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9.

The comparison has limits. Joseph was a real man with faults, and his refusal of Potiphar's wife is one act of faithfulness, not a sinless life. Christ is not merely a greater Joseph but the one whose obedience saves Joseph's descendants. What Joseph shows in a single chapter, faithfulness under temptation and patience under injustice, Christ shows in His whole life, and He gives His own righteousness to those who fail where Joseph stood.
study.god:
The chapter shows God present with His servant in the worst places. The refrain 'the LORD was with Joseph' is spoken over a slave's life and then over a prisoner's life. This is not a God confined to Canaan or to holy places. Jacob had once said at Bethel, 'Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it,' Genesis 28:16; here the narrator affirms that the LORD is in Egypt, in an Egyptian household and in Pharaoh's prison. As Psalm 139:8 puts it, even 'if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.'

God's presence is shown by its effects. The chapter never records God speaking or appearing to Joseph. Instead His presence is seen in what others notice: 'his master saw that the LORD was with him,' verse 3. God is the one who gives success, verses 3 and 23, favour, verses 4 and 21, and kindness, verse 21. The unseen God is visible in the fruitfulness of His servant.

The chapter also shows God's blessing reaching beyond His own people. The LORD blesses 'the Egyptian's household on account of him,' verse 5, both in house and field. God's purpose to bless the nations through Abraham's family, Genesis 12:3, is at work here in small form. God's goodness to Potiphar is not deserved and is not even recognised as coming from the God of Israel; it flows simply because Joseph is there.

Joseph's words in verse 9 teach something essential about God: sin is first of all against Him. 'How could I do such a great evil and sin against God?' Adultery would have wronged Potiphar, and Joseph says so, but he names God as the one ultimately offended. David later confesses the same truth: 'Against You, You only, have I sinned,' Psalm 51:4. God is the holy Lord of every relationship, and His law holds even in a house where no one else acknowledges Him.

The chapter also holds together God's presence and human suffering, a tension it does not resolve. The LORD is with Joseph, and Joseph is still falsely accused and imprisoned. God does not prevent the injustice, but He does not abandon His servant in it, and He shows him chesed, steadfast love, in the prison itself. Genesis 50:20 will later show that God was working through the injustice as well as in spite of it.

For worship, this chapter invites trust and integrity. Believers are called to live before God in private as in public, knowing that He sees, and to believe that His presence is real even when their circumstances look like abandonment. The God who was with Joseph in the dungeon has promised, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you,' Hebrews 13:5.

crossReferences.note: The last verse of chapter 37 says Joseph was sold to Potiphar, and Genesis 39:1 repeats it almost word for word. The repetition shows that chapter 38 is a deliberate interlude and resumes the story exactly where it left off, now to show what God was doing in Egypt.

God promised Jacob at Bethel, 'I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go.' Genesis 39 shows that promise extended to Jacob's son in Egypt. The presence promised to the patriarchs goes with Joseph into slavery and into prison.

Joseph later tells his brothers that God sent him ahead to save lives, and that God made him lord of Pharaoh's household. The injustice of Genesis 39, which placed him in the royal prison among Pharaoh's officials, was one step on the path God used to bring him there.

The psalm adds that Joseph's feet were bruised with shackles and his neck placed in irons 'until his prediction came true.' It shows the harshness of the prison that Genesis 39 passes over, and interprets the time as testing by the word of the LORD.

Proverbs describes the adulterous woman's persuasion and the young man who follows her 'like an ox going to the slaughter.' Genesis 39 gives the opposite picture: a young man urged day after day who refuses and runs. Joseph is the wise son of Proverbs in narrative form.

Paul commands, 'Flee from sexual immorality,' and grounds it in the truth that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and that believers were bought at a price. Joseph's flight from Potiphar's wife, leaving his cloak behind, is the classic biblical example of such fleeing.

David confesses, 'Against You, You only, have I sinned.' Joseph in Genesis 39:9 refuses sin on the same principle before the fact: sexual sin against another person is first of all sin against God. David learned after falling what Joseph held to before temptation.

'God had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official.' Like Joseph in the prison, Daniel is a young Hebrew in a foreign court, and the favour he receives from a pagan official is attributed to God. The two stories share the pattern of faithful exiles blessed in hostile settings.

Christ 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.' Joseph's resistance under persistent temptation is a partial picture of what Christ achieved completely. Because Jesus faced temptation and did not fall, He can sympathise with those who face it now.

Peter commends enduring 'the pain of unjust suffering' because one is conscious of God, and points to Christ, who did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to God. Joseph's silent acceptance of an unjust sentence, with God still with him, fits Peter's teaching exactly.

Stephen says of Joseph that 'God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles' and granted him favor and wisdom. He repeats the refrain of Genesis 39 and shows that the early church read Joseph's story as a pattern of God's presence with a rejected servant.

'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.' The promise God made to His people is the heart of Genesis 39. Joseph's circumstances fell twice, but the LORD's presence did not, and believers are given the same assurance.

study.oneStory:
In the Bible's story of creation, fall, redemption and new creation, Genesis 39 echoes the garden and answers it. In Eden the woman saw that the fruit was 'pleasing to the eyes,' Genesis 3:6, and took it, and the man who was with her ate. In Potiphar's house a woman casts her eyes on Joseph and says 'Sleep with me,' and the man refuses, naming God as the reason. Where Adam gave in to the voice beside him, Joseph does not. The chapter does not reverse the fall, but it shows a son of Abraham living, in one crucial moment, by the word of God rather than by desire.

It also carries forward the promise that Abraham's seed would bring blessing to the nations. Potiphar's house is blessed because Joseph is in it, and soon all of Egypt, and the surrounding lands, will be kept alive through him. The descent of Israel into Egypt, which this chapter advances, will become the setting for the exodus, the Old Testament's great act of redemption.

The chapter also sets up the long pattern of God's people suffering unjustly in foreign places while He remains with them. Daniel in Babylon, the exiles by the rivers, and the church scattered among the nations all live in Joseph's position. Their hope rests in the same presence.

In Christ that presence becomes flesh. Immanuel is God with us, and He goes where Joseph went and further, falsely accused, counted among criminals, brought down to death, and raised to the right hand of the Father. He is not only the example of faithfulness under temptation but the one who has conquered sin for His people.

The new creation brings the refrain of this chapter to completion. The voice from the throne says, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. The presence that went with Joseph into a prison will one day fill a world where there are no prisons, no false accusations and no more tears.

quiz.q: What does the refrain the LORD was with Joseph mean, given where the chapter ends?

options.text: God's presence brought favor and fruitfulness even in slavery and prison, not freedom from hardship.
options.note: The refrain frames a chapter that ends in a dungeon, ruling out ease as the blessing.

options.text: God guaranteed Joseph a comfortable and trouble-free life.
options.note: Joseph's life is full of trouble; the blessing is God's presence, not comfort.

options.text: God was with Joseph only while he was prospering, then left him.
options.note: The refrain returns in prison, showing God stayed with him throughout.

options.text: God's presence made Joseph immune to temptation and accusation.
options.note: He was tempted and falsely accused; God's presence sustained him through both.

quiz.q: On what grounds did Joseph refuse Potiphar's wife?

options.text: It would be a great evil and a sin against God, as well as a betrayal of his master.
options.note: His purity flowed from reverence for God, verse 9.

options.text: He was simply afraid of being caught and punished.
options.note: Fear of consequences is not his stated reason; he names sin against God.

options.text: He found Potiphar's wife unattractive.
options.note: The issue is moral and God-centered, not personal preference.

options.text: He was indifferent and did not care either way.
options.note: He refused firmly and repeatedly, day after day.

quiz.q: How does the motif of Joseph's garment develop the story?

options.text: For a second time a garment of his is seized and used to lie about him.
options.note: First the bloodied robe, now the cloak, marking him as the falsely accused.

options.text: His cloak proves his innocence to Potiphar at once.
options.note: The cloak is used against him, not to clear him; he is imprisoned.

options.text: The garment is a reward from Pharaoh for his service.
options.note: That royal clothing comes later; here the cloak becomes false evidence.

options.text: The garment plays no meaningful role in the chapter.
options.note: It is central, the very object twisted into a lie against him.

quiz.q: How is Joseph in this chapter a picture of Christ?

options.text: The righteous servant who resists sin, is falsely accused, and suffers with God still present.
options.note: The pattern mirrors Christ's innocence, false charges, and the Father's presence.

options.text: A ruler who overthrows Egypt by military conquest.
options.note: That is not this chapter; the likeness is innocent suffering, not conquest.

options.text: A tempter who leads others into sin.
options.note: Joseph resists temptation; he does not tempt others.

options.text: A man who compromises to escape prison.
options.note: Joseph refuses to compromise, and it costs him prison.

quiz.q: What deeper good does the chapter hold out to believers who suffer unjustly?

options.text: The abiding presence of God, who is with His people in every pit and cell.
options.note: God's nearness, not circumstance, is the true blessing, echoed in Hebrews 13:5.

options.text: The promise that the faithful will never face injustice.
options.note: Joseph faces deep injustice; the promise is God's presence, not immunity.

options.text: The assurance of immediate rescue from every trial.
options.note: Joseph's vindication takes years; God is present long before release comes.

options.text: The guarantee of wealth for the godly.
options.note: Joseph is a slave and prisoner; the good is God with him, not riches.

questions: Joseph called adultery a sin against God, not just against people. How would seeing your temptations first as matters between you and God reshape the way you resist them?
The LORD was with Joseph in the slave house and the prison. Where do you most need to believe that God is present with you right now, even in an unjust or confining place?
Joseph fled temptation rather than reasoning with it. What would practical fleeing look like for you, and where do you tend to linger instead?
Joseph did the right thing and it cost him his freedom. How do you keep trusting God when obedience seems to make your situation worse, not better?
Joseph's innocent suffering points to Christ, who was falsely accused for you. How does gazing at the greater Sufferer strengthen you to stay faithful in your own trials?

translationNotes.note: Successful renders a Hebrew word for prospering or accomplishing; in context it describes fruitfulness under God's hand while Joseph is a slave, not material ease.
Make sport of us carries a mocking, contemptuous sense; Potiphar's wife plays on ethnic prejudice by stressing that Joseph is a Hebrew brought among them.
The prison where the king's prisoners were confined was likely attached to the captain of the guard's own house, which sets up Joseph's contact with Pharaoh's officials in the next chapter.
